selected.title: 'Battery cowboys' accused of gaming taxpayer-funded scheme
selected.summary: Almost 100 whistleblower tip-offs claim dodgy operators are rorting a multi-billion-dollar taxpayer-funded solar battery program by mocking up installs, forging signatures and using unlicensed tradies for cash jobs.
selected.why: Major whistleblower allegations regarding fraud in a multi-billion-dollar taxpayer-funded subsidy scheme.
selected.fullText: Whistleblowers accuse solar battery installers of fraud, misconduct in federal rebate scheme - ABC News Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC news iview listen Loading ABC News News Home Whistleblowers accuse solar battery installers of fraud, misconduct in federal rebate scheme Share Share article Whistleblowers accuse solar battery installers of fraud, misconduct in federal rebate scheme By national consumer affairs reporter Michael Atkin and the Specialist Reporting Team's Lucy Kent Topic: Energy Industry Posted Wed 9 Sep 2026 at 4:40am Wed 9 Sep 2026 at 4:40am Wed 9 Sep 2026 at 4:40am , updated Wed 9 Sep 2026 at 1:11pm Wed 9 Sep 2026 at 1:11pm Wed 9 Sep 2026 at 1:11pm Allegations of fraud and misconduct were contained in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. ( ABC News: Craig Hansen ) In short: Allegations of fraud and misconduct have been revealed in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. The untested claims were obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information request. What's next? Shadow Minister for Energy Dan Tehan is calling for an independent Senate inquiry into the revelations. abc.net.au/news/solar-battery-scheme-allegations-fraud-misconduct/107098044 Link copied Share Share article There are fresh claims a multi-billion-dollar taxpayer-funded program to encourage households to install solar batteries is being rorted by unscrupulous operators. They are accused of mocking up installs, forging signatures, using unlicensed tradies for cash jobs and leaving customers with unsafe or broken systems. The allegations of fraud and misconduct were contained in tip-offs sent to the federal watchdog overseeing the Albanese government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. These untested claims were obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, which did not detail any regulatory action that may be underway. The federal scheme offers up to 30 per cent of the cost of solar battery systems. ( ABC News: Michael Lloyd ) The Cheaper Home Batteries Program offers a generous subsidy for households — up to 30 per cent of the cost of solar battery systems. Australians have rushed to sign up, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025. The program is estimated to cost more than $7.2 billion over four years — about $5 billion more than originally announced. reason: Fraud allegations in a $7.2B subsidy scheme raise testable questions about program design accountability versus implementation failure
angle: Subsidy fraud reflects poor regulatory architecture, not inherent subsidy invalidity, and can be fixed without abandoning the program's climate goals.
